notes: 15 courses total (3 lower-division + 12 upper-division). Highly flexible: upper-division includes a self-designed concentration of 6-9 courses (Language, History, Media, or Region), with remaining electives filling out to twelve upper-division courses. Secondary-language requirement is in a language different from that of the primary literature. Structure corroborated by catalog; exact per-concentration course lists not fully itemized.

buckets.label: Lower-division foundation
buckets.note: Three lower-division courses via one of several pathways, e.g. LTCS 50 and 52 plus a third literature course; or a three-course literature/language sequence (e.g. LTFR 2A-B-C); or a college humanities sequence (HUM/MMW/DOC/CAT).

buckets.label: Upper-division concentration
buckets.note: 6-9 courses in one concentration: Language (single non-Anglophone language), History (literature prior to 1800), Media (film/TV/digital/music), or Region (Africa, the Americas, Asia, Mediterranean, Europe).

buckets.label: Upper-division comparative breadth
buckets.note: One Literatures of the Americas (LTAM), one Literatures of Europe (LTEU), and one additional from LTAF/LTAM/LTEA/LTEU/LTWL.

buckets.label: Upper-division electives
buckets.note: Remaining upper-division electives from any Literature subject to reach twelve upper-division courses (count depends on concentration size of 6-9).

buckets.label: Secondary-language requirement
buckets.note: At least one course in a secondary language or literature (taught in a language different from that of the primary literature). Confirmed on catalog.ucsd.edu/curric/LIT-ug.html: 'At least one course in a secondary language or literature; that is, a course taught in a language different from that of the primary literature.' Satisfied by completing the lower-division language sequence in a secondary language through its terminal course (e.g. LTFR 2C, LTSP 2C/2E/3F, LTGM 2C, LTRU 2B; also available in ASL, Classical Greek/Latin, Hebrew, Italian, Korean, Chinese), OR by an upper-division literature course taught in the secondary language. Not a fixed single course, so classified as proficiency; listed courses are representative terminal-course demonstrators, not an exhaustive set. The one hard constraint is that the language must differ from the student's primary-literature language.
